explanations.explanation: That's it, baker. Ezekiel is living in exile, far from home, and then "In visions of God He took me to the land of Israel…" (Ezekiel 40:2). He doesn't just visit the land, either. The LORD sets him on a very high mountain. I spent years stuck in a drawer, so I know what it's like to get carried somewhere better.

Egypt is a good guess, friend, since it's a famous place in the Bible. But the text says the LORD took Ezekiel "…to the land of Israel…" (Ezekiel 40:2). Ezekiel is an exile, so he's been away from that land. This vision takes him to it and sets him on a very high mountain.

Nineveh is another place the Bible talks about a lot, but it isn't on this map. Ezekiel 40:2 says the LORD took him "…to the land of Israel…" in visions of God. Then He set him on a very high mountain. On its southern slope was a structure that resembled a city, so you were close on the city part.

explanations.answer: A linen cord and a measuring rod
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker! The man was "…standing in the gateway with a linen cord and a measuring rod in his hand." (Ezekiel 40:3). Those are measuring tools. Right away that tells you he's here to measure something. My own measuring tools are a scoop and a squint, so I respect the upgrade.

explanations.answer: A scroll and a writing reed
explanations.explanation: A scroll and a writing reed would make him a writer. But Ezekiel 40:3 puts a "…linen cord and a measuring rod…" in his hand. Those are for measuring, not writing. I think that's your first clue that numbers are coming, and plenty of them.

explanations.answer: A trumpet and a burning lamp
explanations.explanation: A trumpet and a lamp would make quite an entrance, friend. But the text says he held "…a linen cord and a measuring rod…" (Ezekiel 40:3). He's standing in the gateway with measuring tools. No music, no light show, just a man who's ready to measure.

explanations.answer: To see everything the man will show him
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The man says, "…pay attention to everything I am going to show you, for that is why you have been brought here." (Ezekiel 40:4). Ezekiel's job is to look and listen closely. When the whole trip is about seeing, you'd better not blink.

explanations.answer: To build a new city on the mountain
explanations.explanation: Building a new city sounds like big work, friend. But the man never gives Ezekiel a building job. He says Ezekiel was brought here to pay attention to everything he's going to show him (Ezekiel 40:4). Ezekiel is there to see, and the structure that resembled a city was already on the slope.

explanations.answer: To guard the gateway with the man
explanations.explanation: Guard duty would be a very different trip. The man's words are, "look with your eyes, hear with your ears, and pay attention to everything I am going to show you, for that is why you have been brought here." (Ezekiel 40:4). Ezekiel is the one being shown things. His reason for being there is to see and hear what the man shows him.

I see why you picked it, friend, but it's the other way around. The man tells Ezekiel, "Report to the house of Israel everything you see." (Ezekiel 40:4). So Ezekiel is supposed to tell people what he sees, not keep it to himself. If I saw all of this, I couldn't keep it in either.
Right, baker. The man says, "Report to the house of Israel everything you see." (Ezekiel 40:4). So Ezekiel is told to share it. Keeping it to himself is the opposite of what the man says.
East is right, baker. "Then he came to the gate facing east and climbed its steps." (Ezekiel 40:6). That's the first gate he measures. After that comes the threshold, which is one rod deep.

West is a fair guess, friend, but it's not the one. The text says the man "…came to the gate facing east and climbed its steps." (Ezekiel 40:6). He starts there, and he measures the threshold first. The gates come in later with different directions, so keep your compass handy.

North does show up in this passage, so you're not far off. But the first gate is the one "facing east" (Ezekiel 40:6). The north gates come later, once the man has finished the east one and moved into the outer court. Order matters on this tour.

explanations.answer: Brings him into the outer court
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. "Then he brought me into the outer court…" (Ezekiel 40:17). Ezekiel just watched a whole gate get measured, and now he's led inside to chambers and a pavement laid out all around, with thirty chambers facing the pavement. I think Ezekiel's feet need a nap by now. That man has a rod in his hand and ground to cover.

explanations.answer: Sends him back down the mountain
explanations.explanation: The tour isn't over yet, friend. After the east gate, the text says, "Then he brought me into the outer court…" (Ezekiel 40:17). The man isn't sending Ezekiel anywhere. He's leading him deeper in, and there's plenty more to see.

explanations.answer: Leaves him waiting at the east gate
explanations.explanation: Waiting at the gate would be a long, boring day. But the man takes Ezekiel along with him. "Then he brought me into the outer court…" (Ezekiel 40:17). I can tell you from my drawer years that waiting is no fun, so I'm glad Ezekiel gets to keep walking.

That's the one, baker. "Next he brought me into the inner court through the south gate…" (Ezekiel 40:28). Then the man measures it, and it matches the others. Measure, match, repeat. I wish every batch I'd stamped had come out that consistent.

The east gate was the first one the man measured, so it makes sense that it stuck in your head. But the text says he brought Ezekiel into the inner court "…through the south gate…" (Ezekiel 40:28). The east gate of the inner court comes after that. The man goes around the inner court in a certain order.

The north gate does get its turn, friend. It just comes later. Ezekiel 40:28 says the man brought him into the inner court "…through the south gate…" The inner gates on the east and north come after that.

Yes, baker! "There the burnt offering was to be washed." (Ezekiel 40:38). The man points to a chamber with a doorway by the portico in each inner gateway. Even in a vision, somebody has to think about the cleanup. I know that feeling, because a bakery has plenty of dishes too.

Grain is a fair guess, friend, but this verse names a different offering. "There the burnt offering was to be washed." (Ezekiel 40:38). That chamber has a doorway and sits by the portico in each inner gateway. So the word that fits the blank is burnt.

Drink is a fair guess, friend, but this verse names a different offering. Ezekiel 40:38 says, "There the burnt offering was to be washed." That chamber has a doorway and sits by the portico in each inner gateway. So the word that fits the blank is burnt.

That's right, baker. Those tables are "…on which the burnt offerings, sin offerings, and guilt offerings were to be slaughtered." (Ezekiel 40:39). So these are working tables. They're set inside the portico of the gateway, two on each side.

Treasure tables would be fancy, friend. But the text says these tables are for the burnt offerings, sin offerings and guilt offerings, which "…were to be slaughtered." there (Ezekiel 40:39). They're for sacrifices. Nothing is said about treasure.

Laying out garments would be a nice use for a table, but that's not what these are for. Ezekiel 40:39 says the offerings "…were to be slaughtered." on them. That covers the burnt offerings, sin offerings and guilt offerings. The text doesn't say what the priests' clothes were laid out on.

Yes, baker. The man says, "The chamber that faces south is for the priests who keep charge of the temple…" (Ezekiel 40:45). So the south-facing chamber goes with the temple. The next verse gives the other chamber its own job.

Gates have been all over this tour, so I get why they came to mind. But the man says the south-facing chamber is "…for the priests who keep charge of the temple…" (Ezekiel 40:45). Those priests keep charge of the temple. The text doesn't say they have charge of the gates.

The treasury would be a big responsibility, friend, but it doesn't show up in this passage. The man says, "The chamber that faces south is for the priests who keep charge of the temple…" (Ezekiel 40:45). That's the job. The north-facing chamber has a different one.

You've got it, baker. The man says, "…the chamber that faces north is for the priests who keep charge of the altar." (Ezekiel 40:46). The south-facing chamber is for the priests who keep charge of the temple (Ezekiel 40:45). Two chambers, two jobs.

I can see how the two chambers could get mixed up, friend. But the man really does say it: "…the chamber that faces north is for the priests who keep charge of the altar." (Ezekiel 40:46). So the statement is true. The south-facing one is for the priests who keep charge of the temple (Ezekiel 40:45).

explanations.answer: Only they may approach the LORD to minister
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The man says, "These are the sons of Zadok, the only Levites who may approach the LORD to minister before Him." (Ezekiel 40:46). Look at who's getting set apart here: not all the Levites, just Zadok's sons. He says it right after pointing out two chambers in the inner court, one for the priests who keep charge of the temple and one for the priests who keep charge of the altar.

explanations.answer: Only they may live inside the holy city
explanations.explanation: Living arrangements are an interesting idea, friend, but the man doesn't say that. He says the sons of Zadok are "…the only Levites who may approach the LORD to minister before Him." (Ezekiel 40:46). It's about ministering before the LORD. The text doesn't say anything about where they live.

explanations.answer: Only they may stand guard at the outer gates
explanations.explanation: Gate duty is a real job, but the man doesn't give it to them here. He says the sons of Zadok are "…the only Levites who may approach the LORD to minister before Him." (Ezekiel 40:46). That's what sets them apart. The outer gates aren't mentioned.
